entries.narration: Why does Databricks exist at all? Because data teams kept hitting the same walls, and every product the company built is the answer to one of them. On the left is how most teams worked. A data warehouse gave them SQL, transactions and governance, but it was expensive at large volumes and kept the data in its own closed format. A data lake was the opposite: cheap files in cloud storage, at any volume, but with no transactions, no way to update a row, and no schema anyone had to respect. So teams ran both, and copied data between them every night, which meant two versions of every number. In the middle is what Databricks built, in order. The company was founded in two thousand and thirteen by the people who created Apache Spark, so that teams could use Spark without running clusters themselves. In two thousand and nineteen it open-sourced Delta Lake, which adds a transaction log to plain files, so a lake can commit, update and roll back. In two thousand and twenty one its lakehouse paper argued that one copy of the data could serve both worlds. Unity Catalog followed, to govern that copy: names, permissions and lineage, open-sourced in two thousand and twenty four. And since then, serverless compute, Lakeflow and Databricks SQL, to run and operate all of it. This frame is documented history, not a run. On the right is the result, the lakehouse: open files in your own storage, a transaction log over them, one catalog, and any kind of compute on top. A bank hits these walls in exactly this order. So we will build one.

Meet Global Bank, a fictional retail bank with five thousand customers. Nothing here is real: every person, card and account comes from a generator that ships with this course, so every number you see can be reproduced exactly. On the left is who sends the bank its data, and in what shape, because that shape decides everything that follows. The card processor sends authorizations as JSON lines, in a new file every fifteen minutes. The card scheme sends settlements, one file a day, one to three days after each purchase. The core banking system does not send files at all: a change data capture tool watches it and writes every change to a customer or an account as a JSON record. The core system also posts salaries, rent and transfers once a day, the mobile app sends its events hourly, and then there are exchange rates, merchants, chargebacks and requests from the privacy team. In the middle is the lab's real run: two months, September and October, landed as files. Almost six thousand card files alone, holding over three hundred and fifty thousand authorizations. Settlements run into November, because October's last purchases clear after the month ends, and that detail will matter when the regulator asks what we reported. On the right is who needs this data. Finance wants balances and statements every morning. Risk wants fraud flagged within minutes. Branch managers may see only their own region. The regulator wants figures exactly as they were reported, on any past date. And data science wants labelled fraud to train a model. One copy of the data has to serve all five.

How do you organise one copy of the data so it can serve five teams? The common answer on Databricks is the medallion architecture: data moves through layers, and each layer makes a stronger promise than the one before. In every catalog, each layer is its own schema. Landing, on the left, holds the files exactly as they were sent. Here is one of them, a real card authorization from the lab: an id, a card, a merchant, an amount and a time. Landing is kept and never edited, so any table can be rebuilt from it. Bronze promises to be complete: one row for every record received, appended and never changed, plus the file it came from and when it arrived. Only engineers read it. Silver promises to be correct: one row per real thing, typed, de-duplicated and validated, with the rows that fail set aside in quarantine rather than lost. Card transactions, customers with their history, accounts, merchants and exchange rates live here, and risk and data science read them. Gold promises to be ready: tables named for the business and shaped for one use, like daily balances, statements, card spend, fraud flags and the regulator's snapshot. Finance, branches and the regulator read only gold. Underneath, the layers decide more than where a table lives. They decide who may read what, what a full refresh may rebuild, and where personal data is masked. Bronze is never rebuilt, because it is the record of what arrived. And one honest note: this is a convention, not a feature. Beside the layers sit a vault for personal data and a schema for machine learning, and a layer that promises nothing new can be skipped, so reference data goes straight to silver.

This is the bank we will build, on a real Databricks workspace, the free edition, one course at a time. It reads left to right, just like the data. Three source systems send files: the card processor, the card scheme and the core banking system. They land in a volume, as files, in course two. Then the medallion. In bronze, Auto Loader picks up every card file exactly once, in course three, and the clearing and change records arrive as received. In silver, card transactions become settled and constrained in course four, and customers and accounts become current and historical in course five. In gold, balances, statements and the regulator's as-of report come in course eight, and fraud flags, scored within minutes, in course nine. On the right are the people it serves, and they read gold only: finance and branch managers through a dashboard, the regulator with the question what did we report on the thirty first of October, and risk with fraud alerts. Along the bottom is what has to be true of every layer. Course six protects it with Unity Catalog. Course seven declares the whole pipeline instead of running notebooks by hand. Course ten schedules it every night, course eleven ships it from git with tests, and course twelve shows what it costs and keeps it fast. Every output in this course comes from really running the code on the workspace, and nothing is typed by hand. Each section adds one thing the bank needs, and teaches the Databricks feature that does it, at the moment the bank needs it. Let's open the workspace.

Global Bank's data team has a Databricks workspace: the free edition, which is free, serverless only, and meant for learning. We will not click through its web pages. Everything in this course is code and commands, run from a laptop, so every step can be repeated. The first tool is the Databricks command line interface, one small program you install once. Before it can do anything, it has to know two things: which workspace, and who you are. The project's readme, open in the editor, records how. Two environment variables: the workspace's address, and a personal access token. The terminal shows the result. The version command says we are on CLI one point twenty two point one. Auth describe answers the two questions: the host, the user, and that we signed in with a personal access token. Warehouses list is the first real question to the workspace, and it has one SQL warehouse, at the smallest size, two X small. On the right is what each command does. The environment says who and where. The CLI turns the command into a call to the workspace's REST API, over HTTPS, and prints the answer. Below that, the three ways to sign in. Environment variables, which this course uses so every run can be replayed. A profile file, with one named entry per workspace. And databricks auth login, which signs you in through the browser with OAuth, and is the right choice for a person at a keyboard. Whichever you use, the token never goes into the repository. Before we ask the workspace to compute anything, let's see where it would.

Where does our code actually run? A Databricks workspace is really three planes, and this picture is worth keeping in mind for the rest of the course. On the left is the laptop. The CLI sends REST calls, and Databricks Connect, which comes next, sends Spark calls to be run somewhere else. Everything lands first in the control plane, which lives in Databricks' own cloud account. It serves the web app and the REST API, it holds the Unity Catalog metastore with every name, grant and lineage record, and it schedules jobs and pipelines. It decides; it never computes. The work happens in the compute plane. On the free edition all compute is serverless: it also lives in Databricks' account, and starts in seconds instead of minutes. There are two kinds. A SQL warehouse, which runs SQL only, and serverless compute for notebooks, jobs and Databricks Connect, which runs Python and SQL. Then storage, where the data lives. On the free edition, managed tables and volumes go to the workspace's default storage. On a paid workspace, a team can also run classic clusters and keep storage in its own cloud account, and the free edition does not offer that, so this course documents it and never pretends to run it. At the bottom left are the workspace's own answers, asked from the laptop: the host, the user, the workspace id, and that it runs on AWS, then the one starter warehouse. The planes themselves come from Databricks' architecture documentation. On the right, what that means for us: serverless compute, the SQL warehouse, Unity Catalog, jobs and pipelines are all real runs in this course. Classic clusters and your own storage are documented only. Now let's run Spark there.

In the Spark course, Spark ran on our laptop. Here it runs on the workspace, and the code barely changes. The tool is Databricks Connect, one pip package, pinned in requirements dot txt to version eighteen point three, the version that matches the workspace's serverless compute. The terminal makes a virtual environment, activates it, and installs it. In the editor is the whole of session dot py: one function that builds a Databricks session with the serverless option, and gets or creates it. There is no host or token in this file. Like the CLI, it reads them from the environment. Then hello asks the workspace two questions and runs one job. The answers come back. Spark four point two point zero, on serverless. We are the user Ana, and the default catalog is called workspace, which is the free edition's own. That is why the next section creates a catalog of our own instead of writing into it. Last, spark dot range of three dot show: a three row table, numbered zero to two, computed on the workspace. The side pane shows how. Our code uses the same PySpark API as the Spark course. Databricks Connect is a Spark Connect client: it does not run Spark on the laptop at all. It turns each call into a plan, and sends the plan over gRPC to serverless compute, where Spark four point two runs it. Only the result comes back. The table below sorts the lines by where they ran: the SQL and the range ran on the workspace, and only print ran on the laptop. Next, somewhere to keep the bank's data.

Every table on Databricks has a three part name: catalog, schema, then the object itself. A catalog is the top level, the unit you grant access to and separate environments by, so Global Bank's development work gets its own: globalbank underscore dev. In catalog dot py, the create function builds it, then one schema for each layer of the medallion, landing, bronze, silver and gold, then one volume. Every statement says if not exists, so running it twice changes nothing. The terminal shows what the workspace now holds. Six schemas: our four layers, plus default and information schema, which Databricks creates in every catalog by itself. Information schema is a set of read only views describing everything else in the catalog, and we will query it when we protect the data. Then the volume, with its path: slash volumes, globalbank dev, landing, card auths. A volume is the answer to a question every lakehouse has: where do the files go before they are tables? It is a folder in cloud storage, but it has a three part name like a table, and Unity Catalog governs it like one, so the same grants decide who may read the bank's raw files. The table below lines up two names that look alike. Card auths in the landing schema is a volume: files, as the card processor sent them. Card auths in the bronze schema will be a table, made from those files, in a moment. One volume per source keeps the grants simple, and course three adds the rest. Now, the files.

A real bank does not generate its card data. The card processor sends it, and a transfer tool drops the files somewhere. Our stand in for the processor is globalbank sim, the generator from course one, now copied into the project. Land dot sh, in the editor, does what that transfer tool would do for one day. It generates the processor's files for that day into a local landing folder, then copies them, as they are, into the landing volume, with databricks fs cp. The terminal runs it for the first of October. The copy reports ninety three files. Listing the local folder shows how they are named: auths, then the time of the fifteen minute window, zero zero zero zero, zero zero thirty, zero one hundred. A window with no traffic has no file, which is why a day holds ninety three of them and not ninety six. Each file holds JSON lines, one authorization per line, like the record we looked at in course one. And the last command asks the workspace, not the laptop: the volume's folder for the first of October now holds ninety three files too. The side pane traces the trip. The generator writes the files, fs cp moves them into the volume, and nothing changes them on the way. That is landing's promise: the files exactly as the source sent them, so that anything we build later can be rebuilt from here. We have not made a table yet. The files are just files, governed by Unity Catalog, and nothing has read them. That is next.

Now we turn the files into a table. First table dot py reads the volume's folder for the first of October with spark dot read dot json, and saves the result as a table: globalbank dev, bronze, card auths. It runs on serverless compute, through Databricks Connect, like hello did. The terminal shows the table holds five thousand five hundred and sixty nine rows: one for every authorization in those ninety three files. Then its history. Version zero, the operation create table as select, writing those same five thousand five hundred and sixty nine rows. Every change to this table will add a version, and course four uses that history to undo a mistake. The last command asks Unity Catalog about the table. Its format is Delta, and it is managed. Managed means Unity Catalog chose where its files live, in the workspace's storage, and it owns them: dropping the table deletes the files. Underneath, a Delta table is Parquet data files plus a transaction log, which records each version. In the side pane, one more line deserves attention. Spark inferred the type of every column from the JSON, and it read amount as a double, a binary floating point number. For a bank, that is the wrong type. A double cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, so sums of money drift by fractions of a cent. Course three reads the amount as a decimal with two places, and lands every file, not just one day's. For now, Global Bank has a catalog, its four layers, a volume of real files, and its first bronze table.

The card processor never stops. A new file lands every fifteen minutes, all day, every day, and bronze has to keep up. Here is the obvious way to do it, and why it fails. Reread dot py reads every file in the volume, with one spark dot read dot json over every day's folder, and counts what it read. The terminal runs it three times, landing one more day before each run. On the first of October it reads five thousand five hundred and sixty nine rows from ninety three files. After the second day lands, it reads eleven thousand one hundred and thirty two rows from one hundred and eighty six files. After the third, seventeen thousand five hundred and thirty three rows from two hundred and eighty files. The plot puts the problem in one picture. On the left of each pair, the rows each run read. On the right, the rows that were actually new. The new rows stay level at about five and a half thousand a day, while the rows read climb every day. The table says the same in numbers: every run reads every file again. Two months of files would mean reading two months on every run. And reading is only half the problem. If this job appended what it read into a table, every run would write yesterday's rows a second time. What we need is a reader that remembers which files it has already taken, and reads only the rest. That reader is called Auto Loader.

Auto Loader is Databricks' answer to files that keep arriving. In land dot py, the ingest function reads with the cloud files format: a stream, pointed at the volume, with JSON as the file format. Writing it uses a trigger called available now. That means: take every file that has not been processed yet, write it, then stop. So the same streaming code runs like a batch job, once per call, which suits a bank that ingests on a schedule. The checkpoint location is where Auto Loader keeps its memory, in a volume in bronze. The terminal shows it working. Two days were already landed, and the first run writes all of them: zero plus eleven thousand one hundred and thirty two rows. Then the third of October lands, ninety four files, and the second run adds only those: six thousand four hundred and one rows, for seventeen thousand five hundred and thirty three in total. Nothing was read twice. The side pane traces one run. Auto Loader lists the folder, skips every file it has already seen, and appends only the new files' rows to the bronze table. The last command asks the table for its column types, and there is a surprise. Every column is a string, even amount and the authorization time. Auto Loader reads JSON as strings unless told otherwise, and there is an extra column, rescued data, which we will meet soon. First, where does Auto Loader's memory actually live?

Everything Auto Loader remembers lives in its checkpoint, and this lab looks inside. Two days are already in bronze. Running ingest again finds nothing new: eleven thousand one hundred and thirty two plus zero. Listing the checkpoint shows five folders, and the side pane says what each one keeps. Sources is the important one: a record of every file already seen. Offsets records what each batch was about to read, and commits records each batch that finished, so a run that crashes halfway can tell exactly where to resume. Metadata holds the stream's identity, and the schemas folder holds the schema Auto Loader inferred, version by version. Now the experiment. We delete the checkpoint, and run ingest again. Without its memory, the stream believes it has never seen a file, so it reads both days again and appends all eleven thousand one hundred and thirty two rows a second time. Bronze now holds twenty two thousand two hundred and sixty four rows, and every authorization in it is there twice. The plot shows the jump. This is the one rule to take from this section: the checkpoint belongs to the table. Delete one and keep the other, and the table quietly fills with duplicates. In a real bank the checkpoint is never deleted by hand. If you ever need to start a table again, you drop the table and its checkpoint together, and rebuild both from landing, which is exactly why landing keeps every file.

Strings are a safe default, but a bank cannot leave money as text. The fix is one line. In land dot py, HINTS names the two columns we know better than inference does: amount as a decimal with eighteen digits and two after the point, and the authorization time as a timestamp. Ingest passes them to Auto Loader as schema hints. A hint is not a full schema: every other column is still inferred, so a new field from the processor can still arrive. The terminal ingests the first of October, five thousand five hundred and sixty nine rows, and asks for the types again. The table on the right lines them up. In section two, amount and auth ts were strings. Now amount is decimal eighteen two, and auth ts is a timestamp. Card id and status stay strings, which is right: they are identifiers and codes, not numbers. Below, why Auto Loader defaults to strings at all. JSON does have numbers, but it has no decimal type: fifty seven point seven two arrives as a binary number unless we say otherwise, and in course two that is exactly what spark dot read dot json gave us, a double. Auto Loader chooses strings so no value is ever lost to a wrong guess. Hints are how we add what we know. Money exact to the cent, and time as time. From here on, every amount in the bank is a decimal.

On the fifteenth of October the card processor changes its files. Every authorization now carries a new field, wallet type: Apple Pay, Google Pay, or nothing. Nobody told the bank. This is the most common way a pipeline breaks, so let's watch Auto Loader handle it. Land dot sh lands the fifteenth, ninety five files. The first run stops, on purpose. The error is unknown field exception, new fields in record. Auto Loader found a field that is not in its schema, and it stops the stream rather than drop the field without anyone knowing. But before stopping, it updated its schema, and our code prints what it added: wallet type, as a string. The editor shows the two lines that make this work. Merge schema lets the bronze table take a new column. And the except clause catches the stream's exception and prints the reason in two lines, instead of a long stack trace. Then the same command, run again. This time Auto Loader starts with the new schema and writes the day: five thousand five hundred and sixty nine plus five thousand five hundred and ninety two rows. The column list now ends with wallet type. Earlier rows hold null there, which is honest: those files never had the field. This is the default mode, called add new columns: stop once, so a person or a scheduler notices, then carry on with the new column. In course ten the nightly job retries the task, so the stop costs one retry, not a night's data.

A new field is one kind of surprise. A wrong value is another. On the twentieth of October, a partner terminal sends three amounts as text with a comma, the way much of Europe writes a decimal: sixty seven comma seven eight. Our hint says amount is a decimal, and that text cannot be parsed as one. What happens to the row? The terminal lands the twentieth, ninety four files, and ingests it: five thousand six hundred and four new rows. Not one row was dropped, and the stream did not stop. Then rescued dot py, in the editor, looks for rows whose rescued data column is not null, and pulls the original amount out of it. There are three, listed on the right. In each, amount is null, because it could not be parsed, and the rescued column still holds exactly what the partner sent: sixty seven comma seven eight, seventeen comma six six, fifty two comma three seven. That is the rescued data column's job. Any field that does not match the schema is moved there, as JSON, instead of being lost or failing the whole file. The side pane traces one row: a string with a comma, a hint that cannot parse it, and a row that is kept with its original value beside it. Bronze has kept its promise, complete, even for values that are wrong. Deciding what to do with them is silver's job, and in course seven the pipeline sends rows like these to quarantine.

When a number in a report looks wrong, the first question is always: where did this row come from? Bronze should answer that without anyone opening a file. Every file Auto Loader reads carries hidden metadata, and land dot py now keeps two pieces of it on every row. Source file is the file's full path in the volume. Landed at is the time the file arrived there. The terminal ingests the first of October, five thousand five hundred and sixty nine rows, then sources dot py groups the rows by file and shows the three busiest files of the day. The file for quarter past three in the afternoon held one hundred and fifty one authorizations, the one at four o'clock also one hundred and fifty one, and quarter to three one hundred and forty one. Their landed at times are the moment this run uploaded them, which is why the replay of this course masks them: they change every time it runs. The table on the right names the two columns and the question each one answers: which file, and when did it arrive. This is bronze's promise again, complete, and complete includes provenance. Any row in the bank's lakehouse can be traced back to the exact file it came from, and because landing never edits or deletes a file, that file is still there to open. Course six follows the same thread further, with lineage between tables.

Before anything is built on bronze, we prove it is complete. Reconcile dot py counts the same thing two ways, once from the files in the volume and once from the table, and the two have to agree. Three days were landed and ingested. The terminal shows the counts. Two hundred and eighty files in the volume, and two hundred and eighty distinct source files in bronze: every file that landed was ingested, none twice. Seventeen thousand five hundred and thirty three lines in the files, and seventeen thousand five hundred and thirty three rows in bronze: every line became a row. Then the authorizations. Seventeen thousand four hundred and seventy five distinct auth ids, and fifty eight rows sent twice. Those are the processor's resends: the same authorization, sent again in a later file. Bronze keeps both copies on purpose, because its job is to hold what was received, not what was meant. And zero rescued rows in these three days. The side pane writes the checks as equations, and below, what bronze keeps and which course fixes it. The fifty eight resends become one row each in silver, in the next course. Rescued rows are quarantined in course seven. Bronze is now complete, traceable and reconciled: every file once, every line a row, every row with its source. Next, the bank builds on it, and the first thing that lands is a mistake.

Bronze is complete. Now the bank builds its first silver table, card transactions: one row per authorization, the ledger that finance will add up. Ledger dot py, in the editor, posts one day at a time with a MERGE. It reads that day's authorizations from bronze, keeps the first copy of each auth ID, so the processor's resends are posted once, and inserts only authorizations silver does not have yet. The tenth to the thirteenth of October are already posted. The terminal posts the fourteenth: silver now holds twenty nine thousand five hundred rows. Then daily dot py adds up approved card spend in euros, per day. Look at the last line. The fourteenth had four thousand nine hundred and ninety eight authorizations, fewer than any other day, and seven hundred and eighty eight thousand euros of spend, two and a half times a normal day. The plot shows the spike. Nothing failed: the MERGE did exactly what it was told. What happened is in the data. At ten in the morning on the fourteenth, the card processor sent one file with its amounts in cents instead of euros, so every amount in it is a hundred times too large. A bank's reports would now be wrong, and every table built from silver would inherit the mistake. In a folder of plain files, undoing this would mean finding and rewriting the files by hand. A Delta table remembers every version of itself.

Every write to a Delta table is a commit, and every commit makes a new version, recorded in the table's transaction log. History dot py prints that record: one line per version, with the operation that wrote it and how many rows it inserted. Version zero created the empty table. Versions one to four are the MERGEs that posted the tenth to the thirteenth of October, around six thousand and five and a half thousand rows each. Version five is the bad batch: the fourteenth. The table on the right lights the two that matter: four, the last good version, and five, the bad one. And every version can still be read. Daily dot py takes an optional version number, and the editor shows how: VERSION AS OF, added to the table's name. The terminal asks for version four. The answer is the ledger as it was the evening before the batch: four days, each between two hundred and eighty five and three hundred and thirty five thousand euros, and no fourteenth at all. This is called time travel. Delta keeps the files of earlier versions until they are cleaned up, by default for seven days, so a query can read the table as it was. For a bank that is more than an undo button: it is how you answer, later, what a report said at the time. Course eight uses it for exactly that. Here, we use it to put the ledger back.

Reading an old version is one thing. Making it the current one is RESTORE. Restore dot py, in the editor, is one statement: restore the table to a version, here four. The terminal runs it, and it reports one file removed and none restored. That is worth a moment. The bad MERGE had only added a file, so the way back is to take that file out of the table, nothing more. No data was copied and nothing was rewritten. The history, in the second command, shows something just as important: version six, RESTORE. Restoring did not erase version five. It wrote a new version that looks like version four. History only grows, and that is a feature. Whoever has to explain to the regulator what happened on the fourteenth can still read the bad version, and see when, and by what, it was replaced. The side pane draws the three versions: the good one, the bad batch, and the restore that points back to the good one. Daily dot py confirms it: the ledger has four days again, with the same totals as version four. The bank has undone the mistake. Now it needs to make sure the same file cannot get in again.

Undoing a mistake is good. Refusing it is better. Delta tables can carry constraints, rules checked on every row of every write, and a write that breaks one is refused whole. Ledger dot py's create function now adds one, highlighted in the editor: amount in range, amount greater than zero and at most a thousand euros. That limit is illustrative, not a real card rule, but it is the kind of sanity check a bank puts on its ledger: no single card authorization in this bank comes near a thousand euros, and none is zero or negative. Adding the constraint checks every row already in the table, so it can only be added to a table that already obeys it, which ours does, after the restore. Now the same file arrives again, and the terminal posts the fourteenth of October once more. This time the MERGE is refused, with the reason Delta gives: delta violate constraint with values, and the first value that broke it, six thousand nine hundred and eighteen. That is sixty nine euros eighteen, in cents. The history shows the last versions, and they end with the thirteenth of October's MERGE. The refused write did not make a version at all: nothing was half-written, nothing needs restoring. The side pane follows the file: the MERGE, the check on every row, and the refusal. The cost of a constraint is that one bad row refuses the whole file. Course seven's pipeline does better, setting bad rows aside and keeping the good ones.

Real systems write to the ledger from more than one place at once: card posting, the clearing file, corrections. What happens when two writes meet? Writers dot py posts the fifteenth and sixteenth of October at the same moment, on two threads, each a MERGE into the same table. And one of them does not get in, at first. The terminal shows it: one writer committed on its first attempt; the other was refused with delta concurrent append, retried, and committed on its second. This is how Delta works, and why. A transaction does not lock the table. Each writer reads the current version, does its work and writes its new files, unseen, then tries to commit the next version number in the table's log. Only one can have it. The second writer's MERGE had read the whole table, to look for existing auth IDs, and the table it read has changed underneath it, so Delta refuses the commit rather than risk a duplicate. The highlighted lines in the editor are the retry: catch that conflict, read again, and try again. Some conflicts Delta can resolve by itself, when the two writes touch different rows and different files; this one, a whole-table read against a new commit, it cannot. The history shows both MERGEs, versions six and seven, one after the other: never half of each. No lock, no corruption, and one retry. The ledger takes two writers. Next, the clearing file.

An authorization is a promise. The money moves later, when the card scheme's clearing file arrives, one to three days afterwards, saying for each authorization whether it settled, and for how much in euros, or whether it was reversed, which is what a refund looks like. The bank's ledger has to apply that file. Land dot sh and land dot py now handle a second source, the clearing file, a CSV a day, through the same Auto Loader code as the cards. The terminal lands the file for the eleventh of October: five thousand seven hundred and twenty one rows in bronze settlements. Then ledger dot py's new settle function, in the editor, applies it with a second kind of MERGE. When a clearing row matches an authorization, update it: status becomes reversed or settled, and the settled amount in euros and the clearing date are filled in. When it does not match, do nothing. Statuses dot py shows the result. One thousand nine hundred and ninety authorizations settled, for a hundred and sixteen thousand four hundred and forty seven euros, and sixty one were reversed. Most of the file's rows matched nothing, and that is correct: they clear authorizations from before the tenth of October, which this silver table never received. The side pane shows the MERGE's two paths, matched and not matched, and the table, silver by status. Thirty one thousand nine hundred and seventy five authorizations are still waiting for their clearing file, which is normal: it is how the bank knows money is promised but not yet moved.

The settle MERGE updates thousands of rows a day, scattered across every file of the table. A Parquet file cannot be edited in place, so the obvious way to update one row is to rewrite its whole file. For a table this size that would mean rewriting nearly everything, every day. Delta has a better way, deletion vectors. Dv dot py, in the editor, reads the last MERGE's metrics from the table's history. The terminal settles the twelfth of October, then asks. Four thousand one hundred and two rows updated. One file added. Zero files removed. One deletion vector added. Here is what that means, drawn on the right. The old data files were not rewritten at all. Each got a deletion vector: a small bitmap saying which of its rows have been replaced. The updated rows, all four thousand of them, were written once, into one small new file. A reader takes each file, skips the rows its vector marks, and adds the new file. A write that touches a few rows in many files becomes cheap, and the table's features confirm deletion vectors are on, by default, for new tables on Databricks. The cost is paid later: readers do a little more work until the table is compacted, which rewrites files without their marked rows. Course twelve looks at who does that, and when. The last section of this course is about the readers that come after silver.

Silver is not the end of the line. Gold tables, reports and other systems read it, and after every settle they need to know what changed: not the whole table again, just the rows the MERGE touched. Delta can record that, as a change data feed. Ledger dot py turns it on with one table property, delta dot enable change data feed, named in the note on the right. From then on, every write also records its row-level changes. The terminal settles the thirteenth of October, and changes dot py reads the feed for that MERGE with the function table changes. The first line counts what it recorded: six thousand and forty one update post-images and six thousand and forty one pre-images. An update is two rows in the feed: the row before, and the row after. The lines below show two authorizations, each as a pair. Before: approved, no settled amount. After: settled, fifteen euros twenty three, and eighty euros seventeen. Inserts and deletes appear the same way, as one row each, with their change type. A reader that remembers the last version it processed can ask for everything since, and get exactly the rows to apply, which is how incremental processing downstream stays cheap. Silver card transactions is now trustworthy: it can be undone, it refuses bad files, it takes concurrent writers, it settles, and it tells its readers what changed. Next, the bank's other silver tables: its customers and accounts.

Card authorizations are events: each one happens once and never changes. Customers and accounts are different. They live in the bank's core system, and they change: people move, their identity checks are reviewed, accounts open and close. The core system does not send the bank a copy of every customer every night. A change data capture tool, CDC for short, watches its database and writes one record per change. The landing volume now holds September and the first nine days of October of those records, and Auto Loader takes them into bronze with the same code as the cards: twelve thousand one hundred and fifty seven changes. Record dot py counts them, by table and operation. Five thousand and sixty four customer inserts, five hundred and seventy one customer updates, six thousand four hundred and ninety nine account inserts, and twenty three account deletes. Then it takes one change apart. The table on the right reads it field by field. Op is U, an update. Seq is the core system's own commit order, twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five: remember that number. Ts is when it changed, table says which core table, and key says which row. After holds the whole row as it is after the change, here a new address, one hundred and thirty six River View. Notice that bronze kept after as JSON text, exactly as received. Turning it into typed columns is silver's job, and that is next.

Silver dot customers should answer one question: who is each customer right now. Cdc dot py builds it with a MERGE, applied one batch of change files at a time. A batch is just the files whose path matches a pattern. For each batch, the code keeps only the latest change per customer, ordered by seq, newest first, and parses the after column with from JSON into typed columns. Then the MERGE: a customer silver already has is updated, a new one is inserted, and a D deletes the row. This is called slowly changing dimension type one: the current state, with no history kept. The terminal applies two batches. September first: five thousand and forty four changes, all inserts, because the first day is the core system's initial snapshot. Silver now holds five thousand and forty four customers. Then the first to eighth of October: one hundred and twenty five changes, seventeen new customers and one hundred and eight updates, for five thousand and sixty one rows. The side pane shows the flow, and the table puts the two batches side by side. This works, for as long as the changes arrive in the order they happened. On the ninth of October, they do not.

On the ninth of October, customer C000001 moves twice in one day. The core system commits two changes: sequence twelve thousand one hundred and forty eight, to six River View, and later sequence twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five, to one hundred and thirty six River View. But the CDC tool writes two files that day, one at noon and one just before midnight, and it puts the later change in the earlier file. This happens in real systems more often than anyone would like. The terminal applies the two files in the order they arrived, with the MERGE from the last section. Twelve changes, then thirteen. Then customer dot py, in the editor, lists every change for C000001 in arrival order, and silver's row now. The table on the right is the same list. Silver says six River View, sequence twelve thousand one hundred and forty eight. That is wrong. The customer has already left that address; the newest change is twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five. The second table shows the two orderings and their two answers. Applied by arrival, the older change wins, because it was written last. Applied by sequence, the newer one wins, as it should. Statements and cards would now be posted to an address the customer no longer lives at. The fix is one condition.

The fix lives in the MERGE itself. Silver now stores the sequence number of the change that wrote each row, and both matched clauses gain one condition: s dot seq greater than t dot seq. A change may only replace a row written by an older change. Here are the same two files again, applied in the same wrong order. The first file writes C000001 with sequence twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five, the newest. When the second file arrives, its change for C000001 carries twelve thousand one hundred and forty eight, older than the row it would replace, so the condition is false and the row is left alone. Look at the counts: the second file held thirteen changes, and this time only eleven rows were updated, one fewer than before, plus one insert. And customer dot py now says sequence twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five, one hundred and thirty six River View. The side pane follows the skipped change step by step. This is the general rule for any change feed: order by the source's own sequence, never by arrival. Arrival order is a property of the delivery, not of the data. Course seven's pipeline does the same with a setting called sequence by.

Accounts close. When one does, the core system sends a change with op D, a key, and no after at all, because there is nothing after. Cdc dot py now knows two tables. The editor shows the new entry: accounts, keyed by account id, with their columns, including the IBAN and the overdraft limit. The terminal applies September: six thousand four hundred and seventy four changes, six thousand four hundred and fifty four accounts inserted. Some accounts that opened and closed inside September never reach silver at all, because the latest change for them is the delete. Then October's first nine days: twenty eight changes, twenty five inserts, and three deletes. Silver dot accounts ends with six thousand four hundred and seventy six rows. Closed dot py asks the other side of the question. Bronze still holds all twenty three D records, and not one of those accounts is in silver. The side pane draws the split. Silver answers what is true now, so the row goes. Bronze answers what happened, so the record stays, with its file and its sequence. If a regulator asks when an account closed, the answer is in bronze. Silver's own history of a row is the next step.

Silver dot customers knows who each customer is now. But a bank is constantly asked who a customer was on a date: which address a card was sent to, what their identity check said when a payment went through. That needs history, kept as its own table. Scd2 dot py builds silver dot customers underscore history from bronze. Every change becomes one row, a version of the customer, and each version holds from its own timestamp until the next change for the same customer. That next timestamp comes from the window function lead, ordered by seq. The latest version has no end, so it is the current one. This is slowly changing dimension type two. The terminal builds it: five thousand six hundred and thirty five versions of five thousand and sixty four customers. Then it prints C000001's timeline, drawn on the right. Verified on the first of September. Marked for review on the sixth. Then the two moves of the ninth: six River View for under two hours, and one hundred and thirty six River View from then on. Because the history is ordered by sequence, not by arrival, the pair that arrived the wrong way round is in the right order here, with no special handling. Silver now has two customer tables for two questions: who now, and who when.

Here is the question that history exists for. Risk is reviewing card payments from the end of September, and needs each payer's identity check status when they paid, not today. Pit dot py joins every payment from the twenty eighth to the thirtieth of September to its customer twice. The first join, to silver dot customers, gives the status now. The second, to the history, picks the one version whose valid from is at or before the payment, and whose valid to is after it or still open. That is a point-in-time join. The terminal runs both. Of sixteen thousand seven hundred and nine payments, one hundred and seventy were made by customers whose status has changed since. The rows on the right are the first of them: customers who were verified when they paid, and are now pending or under review. Join to the current table, and a review would conclude these payments were made by unverified customers. They were not. The status changed after. Every report that asks about the past, and in a bank that is most of them, has to join to history this way. In course eight, the regulator asks a different version of the same question, about the bank's own reports.

Everything in this course started from files a CDC tool had written. That is one common way for a bank to feed a lakehouse, and it is the one we could run here. There is another. Lakeflow Connect, part of Databricks, offers managed connectors that read a source system themselves. For databases such as SQL Server, PostgreSQL and MySQL, a managed connector reads the database's change log through an ingestion gateway, and an ingestion pipeline writes the changes into a streaming table, with history tracking, type one or type two, as a setting. The top row is what this course built, and ran on the workspace: the core database, a CDC tool, the landing volume, our own Auto Loader and MERGE code, and silver. The bottom row is the managed connector's shape, from the Databricks documentation, which we checked while writing this course. It is not run here: the free edition has no core banking database of ours to connect to. The table compares the two. With files, a vendor's tool reads the source, and ordering and deletes are your code's job, as sections three to five showed. With a connector, Databricks reads the source and handles both. Either way, the lessons hold: order by the source's sequence, keep deletes as history, and keep the current state and its history apart. Next, the bank has customers' names, national IDs and IBANs in its lakehouse, and they need protecting.

Silver now holds people: names, national IDs, dates of birth, addresses and account numbers. Before anyone else reads it, the bank has to decide who may see what, and Databricks decides that in one place: Unity Catalog. Here is its model, with the workspace's own answers in the terminal below. At the top is the metastore, one per region; the free edition has exactly one. It holds catalogs. We list only ours, filtered to names that start with globalbank, because a real workspace holds other people's catalogs too, and a governance lesson should not print them. The owner of globalbank dev is Ana, who created it, and an owner may grant. Inside the catalog are the schemas, one per layer, and the lab counts what each holds right now: three volumes in landing, bronze's table and its checkpoint volume, and silver's two tables, customers and accounts. Two schemas are new in this course: governance, which will hold the rules, and vault, which will hold personal data apart. The third column says who each layer is for. On the right, what Unity Catalog governs: grants, which say who may read a schema or a table; masks and row filters, which decide what each reader sees inside one; and tags, lineage and audit, which say what a column holds, where a table came from, and who read it. Every read, from a notebook, a job, or Databricks Connect on a laptop, goes through these rules. The rest of this course sets them, one at a time.

The first rule is the coarsest: who may read which layer. Grants dot sql writes the bank's policy as code. Engineers may use the catalog, and read bronze and silver. Risk reads silver, because investigations need row-level detail. Finance and the branches read gold only: finished products, never raw data. The table on the right is that matrix. Govern dot py applies the file one statement at a time and reports each one. And on the free edition, every grant is refused, with the reason principal does not exist. That is honest, and worth understanding. Unity Catalog grants to account-level groups, which a bank syncs from its identity provider, with a protocol called SCIM. The free edition has no account console and no SCIM, and a group created inside the workspace is not an account group, so these four groups cannot exist here. On a paid workspace, this file is the whole job: run it, and the layers are closed to everyone the matrix leaves out. Notice the shape of the policy, too. Grants follow the medallion, layer by layer, which is one more reason to keep one schema per layer. But grants are all or nothing: a reader either sees a table or does not. A bank also needs readers who may see a table but not every column of it. That is a mask.

Risk needs national IDs and IBANs whole. Most other readers of silver need customers, but not those two columns. A column mask solves this inside the table itself. Masks dot sql does three things. It creates governance dot roles, a small table that says which role each user reads as. It creates a function, unless risk, which returns the value whole if the current user's row says risk, and otherwise only its last three characters behind stars. And it attaches that function to two columns: national ID in silver customers, and IBAN in silver accounts. The terminal applies it, four statements, all accepted. Peek dot py, the same small query every time, reads two customers. With no role, the national IDs and IBANs come back masked, in the first table. Then roles dot py records that Ana reads as risk, and the very same query returns them whole, in the second. Nothing about the query changed. The side pane shows who decides: the query reads the column, the mask runs on every read of it, and the mask asks the roles table. A note on the roles table. The usual way to write this is with group membership, but the free edition has no account groups, so this course uses a mapping table, which is also a documented pattern, and lets one user show two readers. Masks change what a reader sees in a column. The next rule changes which rows they see at all.

A branch manager in the North region should see the North's customers, and no one else's. That is a row filter. Filters dot sql creates a function, my region, which keeps a row if the current user reads as risk, or if their role's region matches the row's region. Then it sets that function as the row filter of silver customers, on the region column. Like a mask, it runs inside every read, so no query can forget it. The terminal applies it, then switches Ana's role twice. As a branch manager for the North, regions dot py, a plain count of customers by region, sees one region and its customers. As risk, the same script sees all five regions and every customer. The plot puts the two answers side by side: one bar for the North, and five for risk. The numbers on the right are the totals. The table and the query did not change: the filter did the work. Masks and filters together are how one silver table serves several kinds of reader safely, instead of copying it into one table per audience, which is how banks used to end up with a dozen copies of their customers, each a little out of date. Next, the bank needs to know where all of its personal data actually is.

Before anyone can protect personal data, someone has to find it, in every table, including the ones built next year. Unity Catalog lets you tag columns, and query the tags. Tags dot sql classifies every column in silver that identifies a person: national ID, names, date of birth, email, address, and the IBAN, each with a tag called pii and a value saying what kind it is. The terminal applies the seven statements, then pii dot py asks the catalog's information schema for every column tagged pii. The answer, drawn on the right, is the bank's personal data map: seven columns in two tables, and what each one holds. A tag is metadata. It protects nothing by itself, and that is the point the colours make: only the two columns in red, the national ID and the IBAN, are masked so far. The tags make the gap visible. An auditor, or a script run every night, can now compare the tagged columns with the masked ones, and flag any personal column that has no mask. Tags are also how the bank will find the data to delete when a customer asks to be forgotten, which is the last section of this course. Before that, two questions Unity Catalog answers without being asked: where did a table come from, and who has read it.

Every time a query writes a table, Unity Catalog records which tables it read. That record is called lineage, and it is kept as a system table, system dot access dot table lineage, which can be queried like any other. Lineage dot py asks it for every edge into a table of globalbank dev, in the last two hours, for tables that still exist. The terminal prints the edges, and the side pane draws them as a graph. Files in the landing volumes feed bronze: the card authorizations and the core system's changes. Bronze's changes feed silver customers and silver accounts, and the history table. Bronze's card authorizations feed silver card transactions. No one drew this. It was recorded as the code ran, by the platform, from the queries themselves. This is what answers the questions a bank is asked when a number is wrong: which tables does this report depend on, and if this source sends bad data, which tables are affected. Course seven adds a pipeline, and its graph will be drawn the same way, from the platform's own records. Lineage says what was built from what. The next system table says who read it.

Regulators ask banks a simple question that is hard to answer: who looked at this customer's data? Unity Catalog writes an audit event for every request it checks, and keeps them in another system table, system dot access dot audit. Audit dot py asks it about one table, silver customers, in the last hour: who made each kind of request, and how many. Before it ran, this step read the table through regions dot py, the row-filtered count from section four, and the audit log has it. The table on the right is the answer: Ana, and three kinds of request Unity Catalog checked. Get table: every read looks up the table's definition first, the count included. Update tables: the MERGEs that built it. And delete table: this replay's own reset, dropping the table it had before. The exact counts change every run, so the frame reads them from the session, and they are never quoted. The side pane traces one read: the script reads through Databricks Connect, Unity Catalog checks the request against grants, masks and filters, and writes an event, and a few minutes later the event is a row in the system table. Together, lineage and audit are the evidence a regulator asks for. Last in this course, the hardest rule of all: forgetting a customer.

A customer has the right to ask the bank to erase their personal data. The bank also has to keep its records of what happened, for years, under its retention rules. The two meet in silver, and the way to satisfy both is to keep them apart. Vault dot py builds a vault: one table that holds each customer's identifying columns, keyed by customer ID, and nothing else. Facts, such as accounts and card transactions, keep the customer ID only. Then erase dot py reads the privacy team's request, E R twenty twenty six zero zero three one, and deletes that one customer from the vault. The terminal shows what the delete did, and the table on the right shows something important: the version before the delete still holds the customer. Time travel, the feature that saved the ledger in course four, now works against erasure, because the old data files are still there. Silver accounts still holds the customer's account rows, by ID only, which is what retention needs: the facts, without the person. Purge dot py makes the erasure physical. Reorganising the table with purge rewrites the files the deletion marked. Then vacuum removes old files, but only those older than the table's retention period, seven days by default, so nothing is removed today. The erasure is complete when that window has passed. The retention rule in this course is illustrative, not legal advice. The bank's data is now governed layer by layer. But it is still built by a dozen scripts run by hand, and the next course replaces them with one declared pipeline.

By now Global Bank's lakehouse is built by half a dozen scripts: land the files, ingest bronze, post silver, apply the core system's changes, build history. Someone has to run them every night, in the right order. Nightly dot sh, in the editor, is that someone, written down: one script after another, in the order typed. And it is in the wrong order. Posting to silver comes before ingesting bronze. The terminal runs it for the second of October. Silver card transactions reports five thousand four hundred and ninety two rows: exactly what it had before, because the post read bronze before the day's files were in it. Then bronze takes five thousand five hundred and sixty three new authorizations, and the core system's changes land and are applied. Every step succeeded, and the second of October is missing from silver. Nothing failed, so nothing told anyone. Only when someone notices and runs the post again does silver grow to ten thousand nine hundred and eighty three rows. The table on the right puts the order typed beside the order needed; the plot shows silver standing still. The order was never really a choice: each step reads what an earlier one writes, so the reads decide the order. If the platform could see the reads, it could work out the order itself, and never get it wrong. That is what declaring a pipeline means.

A Lakeflow pipeline, built on Spark Declarative Pipelines and formerly called Delta Live Tables, is code that declares tables instead of writing them. Bronze dot py declares two. Each function returns a query, here Auto Loader reading a landing volume, exactly as in course three, and the decorator dp dot table says: this query defines the table bronze card auths. Nothing in the file runs it, or says when, or in what order. Because the query is a stream, the table is a streaming table: each update of the pipeline appends only what is new, and the pipeline keeps its own checkpoints, so there is no checkpoint folder in our code any more. Deploy dot py uploads the file and creates the pipeline, globalbank pipeline: serverless, writing to globalbank dev. Run dot py starts an update, waits for it, and asks each table what it holds. The first update: five thousand five hundred and sixty nine card authorizations, and eleven thousand nine hundred and ninety six change records. Then the second of October lands, ninety three files, and the second update takes only those: bronze card auths grows to eleven thousand one hundred and thirty two, and the change records, with nothing new, stay as they were. The side pane traces it: the code, the pipeline that runs it, and the table it keeps. Bronze is declared. Next, silver and gold, which are not streams at all.

Silver card transactions is not a stream of new rows. It is one row per authorization, so a resend arriving tomorrow changes what today's answer should have been. A query like that is declared as a materialized view: a query whose result the pipeline keeps up to date. Silver dot py declares silver card transactions as bronze, de-duplicated by auth ID, the same rule as course four. Gold dot py, in the editor, declares gold card spend daily: approved spend in euros per day, reading silver only. The terminal deploys the pipeline, now three source files, and runs it. The first update builds everything: silver holds five thousand five hundred and forty nine authorizations, gold has two days. The second of October lands, and the second update brings silver to eleven thousand and ninety nine and gold to three days. The words in brackets come from the pipeline's event log, and say how each view was refreshed. The first time, both were computed completely, since there was nothing to start from. The second time they were not: silver was refreshed incrementally through its window function, and gold through its group aggregate, recomputing only what the new rows touched. The table on the right lines up both updates. Below, the two kinds of dataset. A streaming table appends. A materialized view is a query whose result is kept, and the pipeline decides how cheaply it can keep it current. Three tables in three files, and nobody said in which order to build them.

So how did the pipeline know to build bronze before silver, and silver before gold? It read the queries. Every dataset's definition names the tables it reads, and when an update starts, the pipeline records each flow's inputs and output in its event log, as an event called flow definition. Graph dot py reads those events from the last update and prints every edge: bronze card auths feeds silver card transactions, and silver card transactions feeds gold card spend daily. The side pane draws the same edges as a graph. Nobody wrote this order down, and nobody can get it wrong: change a query to read a different table, and the graph changes with it. This is the answer to the nightly script from section one. That script was an order typed by hand, and silently wrong. Here, the order is derived from the code, every time. The graph is drawn from the pipeline's own record, not from a screenshot of its page in the workspace, which is how this whole course shows what the platform did. Bronze core changes has no edge yet, because nothing reads it so far. It will, in section seven. Before that, the pipeline starts checking the data that passes through it.

Course four put a constraint on silver, and a bad file was refused whole. A pipeline has a finer tool, the expectation: a rule each row is checked against, with a policy for the rows that fail. Silver dot py now declares rules. Currency known only warns: a failing row is kept, and counted. The two in the rules dictionary drop: amount known, because the partner's comma amounts arrive empty, and amount in range, more than zero and at most a thousand euros, the same illustrative limit as before. This time the landing holds the days with every planted problem: the thirteenth and fourteenth of October, with the batch in cents, and the twentieth, with the comma amounts. The terminal deploys and runs, then quality dot py reads the event log for what each expectation saw. Amount in range: eighty one rows failed: the batch in cents, and the three comma rows too, because an empty amount is in no range. Amount known: three failed, the comma rows. Currency known: none. Silver ends with sixteen thousand six hundred and sixty six transactions, and gold is built from those alone. The second table lists the three policies. Warn keeps the row and counts it. Drop leaves it out and counts it. Fail stops the update, which is course four's constraint, in pipeline form. Dropping solves silver's problem, but now eighty one rows have left the bank's books with nothing but a count to remember them by. They need somewhere to go.

A dropped row should not disappear. Someone will be asked about it: the partner whose amounts were empty, the processor whose batch was in cents. So silver dot py declares a second materialized view, card transactions quarantine. It reads the same bronze rows and keeps exactly the ones that break a rule, the opposite of silver's filter, written from the same rules dictionary, so the two can never disagree. It keeps the rescued data column too, the original text the partner sent. The terminal runs the pipeline, and the quarantine holds eighty one rows. Then recon dot py reconciles silver against bronze, the same check course three did for bronze against the files. Bronze holds sixteen thousand seven hundred and ninety seven rows. Silver holds sixteen thousand six hundred and sixty six. The quarantine holds eighty one. And fifty are resends: the same authorization sent twice, kept once. Sixteen thousand six hundred and sixty six, plus eighty one, plus fifty, is sixteen thousand seven hundred and ninety seven, exactly bronze. The side pane draws the three ways a bronze row can go. Every row is accounted for: in silver, set aside with its reason, or recognised as a copy. That is silver's promise, correct, without breaking bronze's, complete. Card transactions are declared. The customers still come from course five's hand-written MERGE, and that is next.

In course five, keeping customers current took a page of code: parse each change, keep the latest per key, a MERGE with a guard against out-of-order changes, deletes, and a separate script for history. A pipeline does all of it in one declaration, called AUTO CDC. Silver dot py first declares a temporary view over bronze's change records, parsing each customer's after column into typed columns, as a stream. Then two declarations, highlighted. Create auto CDC flow, into silver customers: keys customer ID, sequence by seq, delete when op is D, stored as type one. And the same again into silver customers history, stored as type two, tracking address and KYC status. The table on the right maps course five's code to the arguments that replace it: the join key, the sequence guard, the delete clause, and the history script. The terminal runs the pipeline. Silver customers holds five thousand and eighty four customers; the history holds five thousand eight hundred and thirty three versions. And the out-of-order pair from course five? Customer dot py prints silver's row for C000001: sequence twelve thousand one hundred and fifty five, one hundred and thirty six River View. The newest change won, though it arrived first, because sequence by orders by the source's sequence, as we did by hand. Bronze core changes now has edges in the graph, too. The pipeline is the whole medallion. Next, how to see what it did.

Every update of a pipeline writes an event log: what it planned, what it built, how many rows, which expectations failed, and how long each step took. Sections three to six read pieces of it already. Events dot py reads the last update whole. The event log is a table, read with the event log function and the pipeline's ID, so it can be queried like any other: here, grouped by event type, then by flow. The first line counts the busiest kinds of event: flow progress, by far the most, then flow definitions and dataset definitions. Below, one line per flow: its final status, and the seconds from when it started running to its last event. The plot draws those durations. The numbers change on every run, so the frame reads them from the session, and they are never quoted. This is how the course has drawn the pipeline without a single screenshot of its page in the workspace: the graph in section four, the expectations in section five and these timings all come from the same log. In production, the event log is what an alert watches, and what an engineer reads first when the morning's numbers look wrong. Last, the one operation on a pipeline that has to be handled with care.

Sometimes a pipeline's tables have to be rebuilt from scratch: a rule changed, a bug was fixed, and every row must be recomputed with the new code. That is a full refresh. It is safe for silver and gold, which are derived from bronze. It is not safe for bronze, which holds files the sources may never send again: a full refresh empties a streaming table and re-reads its sources, and if the landing zone has been cleaned up, history is gone. So bronze dot py marks both bronze tables with one table property, pipelines dot reset dot allowed, false. The terminal counts the tables, runs a full refresh, and counts again. Bronze card auths: sixteen thousand seven hundred and ninety seven before, and the same after, kept. Silver card transactions, sixteen thousand six hundred and sixty six; silver customers, five thousand and eighty four; gold, five days: all rebuilt from bronze, and arriving at exactly the same numbers, which is itself a test of the pipeline. The table on the right says which layer a full refresh touches, and why. This is the medallion's contract made enforceable: bronze is the record and is never rebuilt, while silver and gold can always be rebuilt from it. Global Bank's lakehouse is now one declared, checked pipeline. Next, it has to serve the business: balances, statements, and a regulator's question.

Silver is correct. Gold is where the bank's questions get answered, and the people asking them, in finance, in the branches, on a dashboard, write SQL, not Python. On Databricks, SQL runs on a SQL warehouse: compute made only for queries, which starts in seconds and stops when nobody is asking. Free Edition has exactly one, and the first command in the terminal asks the workspace about it: the Serverless Starter Warehouse, size two X small, serverless. Warehouse dot py, in the editor, is how this course talks to it from the laptop. It sends a statement through the SDK's statement execution API, waits until it has finished, and prints the result as aligned columns. No Spark session, no cluster: a request over HTTPS, and rows back. The second command runs a SQL file against gold card spend daily, the table the pipeline keeps current since course seven. The twenty ninth of October: five thousand and sixty four approved authorizations, two hundred and eighty six thousand euros. The thirtieth and the thirty first look the same. The handful of rows dated the twenty eighth are authorizations from just before midnight that arrived in the twenty ninth's files. The side pane traces one statement, end to end: the script, the warehouse, the table. From here on, every gold table in this course is a SQL file run this way, and its first one is the number every customer cares about: their balance.

A balance is not stored anywhere in the bank's sources. The core system sends postings: salary, rent, transfers. The card scheme sends what cleared. A balance is what you get when you start from the opening balance and add everything that moved, day by day. Daily balances dot sql says exactly that. It joins every account to every day since it opened, sums what moved each day, postings in and cleared card payments out, and a window function runs the total forward through the days. The result is a plain Delta table in gold, rebuilt by create or replace. The terminal builds it on the warehouse and counts it: three hundred and ninety three thousand five hundred and seven rows, one per account per day, for six thousand five hundred and thirty five accounts, from the first of September to the thirty first of October. The second command reads one account's October, a week to a row. The plot draws it. Account A0000011 starts the month below zero, and rent leaves on the first. Card payments pull it down a little more every few days, to minus two thousand three hundred and fifty one euros. On the twenty fifth the salary arrives and it jumps back to about minus two hundred. This customer is overdrawn for all of October. The averages across the bank are healthy; this account is not, and gold is where that becomes visible. Hold on to it: section six builds the alert that finds accounts like this one.

Every month, every customer gets a statement: what they started with, what came in, what went out, and what they ended with. Monthly statements dot sql builds October's for every account at once. The opening balance is gold daily balances on the thirtieth of September; the closing balance is the same table on the thirty first of October. Between them, card payments that cleared in October, and the core system's salary, rent and transfers, each summed by kind. The terminal builds it and summarises it: six thousand four hundred and forty two statements, an average closing balance of five thousand four hundred and twenty six euros, and five hundred and eighty three accounts closing the month overdrawn. Then account A0000011's statement, a line per entry, in the side pane. Opening balance: minus nine hundred and seventy euros. Card payments: minus one thousand and eighteen. Salary: two thousand one hundred and fifty six. Rent: minus five hundred and nineteen. No transfers. Closing balance: minus three hundred and fifty one. The last line is not an entry. It is a check: the opening, plus everything that moved, minus the closing. It is zero. The statement adds up, and it adds up because both balances come from one table built from the same postings, not from two systems that might disagree. A statement is what the bank says to a customer. Next, what it says to its regulator, and what happens when the numbers move after it has said it.

On the thirty first of October, the bank sends its regulator a report of the card book: for each of the last days of the month, how much was approved, and how much has cleared. Regulatory snapshot dot sql writes it to a gold table. But card payments clear one to three days after they are made, so on the thirty first much of the last days' spending has not cleared yet. Then, on the first, second and third of November, the late clearing files land. The terminal lands three files, runs the pipeline, and rebuilds the report. Months later, the regulator asks: what did you report on the thirty first? The numbers have moved since. Delta keeps every version of the table, and as of dot py, in the editor, reads two of them with timestamp as of. As reported, version zero: of five thousand four hundred and forty nine authorizations on the twenty ninth, three thousand six hundred and seventy seven had cleared, two hundred and three thousand euros. On the thirtieth, one thousand seven hundred and ninety three. On the thirty first, nothing yet. As restated, version one: everything cleared, three hundred and forty three thousand euros on the thirty first alone. Both answers are true, about different moments. The bank can show what it said, and why it changed, from the table itself, without keeping copies. The side pane lines up the two versions.

The people who run the bank do not run SQL files from a laptop. They open a dashboard. A dashboard is a consumer, and consumers read only gold, but the charts this one needs group by each account's region and customer segment, which live in silver. So the first command builds one more gold table, gold accounts: one row per account, with its product, overdraft limit, region and segment. Six thousand five hundred and thirty five accounts, five thousand one hundred and twelve of them current accounts, five regions, three segments. Now the dashboard. On Databricks it is an AI/BI dashboard, still called Lakeview in the API, and like everything else in this course it is a file in the repo: statements dot lvdash dot json, two datasets, each a SQL query on gold, and a bar chart for each. Dashboard dot py, in the editor, creates it in the workspace from that file, publishes it on the warehouse, and then runs each dataset once here, one line each, so this course can draw the charts from their real results instead of a screenshot. October card spend by region: every region between one point eight and two million euros, the West highest at two million and thirteen thousand. The average closing balance by segment: about one thousand two hundred and eighty four euros for three thousand five hundred and thirty two standard accounts, five thousand seven hundred and ninety seven for plus, and seventeen thousand eight hundred and seventeen for the two hundred and thirty four premier accounts. The side pane draws both charts. Next, a question nobody should have to open a dashboard to ask.

Section two found an account that spent all of October overdrawn. A bank does not wait for someone to notice that on a chart: each account has an overdraft limit, and going past it should tell someone the next morning. Overdrawn dot sql is the question, written once: for each day since the twenty fifth of October, how many accounts closed the day below their limit, and how low the lowest one went. It reads gold daily balances and gold accounts, nothing else. The terminal runs it. One hundred and sixty nine accounts were past their limit on the twenty fifth, the day salaries arrive, and the number grows every day after it: two hundred and twenty on the twenty seventh, three hundred and twenty five on the thirty first, the lowest at minus two thousand six hundred and five euros. An answer like this should not depend on someone running a query. Alert dot py, in the editor, turns it into a Databricks SQL alert: the same query text, run on the warehouse on a schedule, every day at seven in the morning, Amsterdam time, with a condition, the sum of the accounts column greater than zero. The alert is created and active. When the condition is true, the alert notifies its subscribers. That part, an email to the owner, is the workspace's to send and is not shown here. The side pane puts the query's real rows beside the rule: query, condition, notification. Gold is now read by a dashboard and watched by an alert. Last in this course: when one of these queries gets slow, how to see why.

Every query in this course has been fast, because the tables are small. A bank's are not, and the first question about a slow query is always the same: how much did it read? The warehouse records every statement it runs in a system table, system query history: who ran it, how long it took, and what it read. Point dot sql asks the question the regulator's report asks most often: card spend on one day, the thirtieth of October. Five thousand six hundred and eighteen settlements, three hundred and eight thousand euros. Slow dot py, in the editor, then reads this session's statements back from the history. One thing to know first: the history arrives some minutes after a statement runs, so the script waits until its own query appears. Then, per statement, the files it read, the files it pruned, and the megabytes. The one day query read one file and pruned one: Delta keeps the minimum and maximum of each column for every file, and the file whose dates could not include the thirtieth was skipped without being opened. The overdraft alert's query read two files and pruned none; so did the dashboard's two datasets: they need every account, so there is nothing to skip. On tables this size that is a megabyte. On a bank's, it is the difference between seconds and minutes. What decides it is how many files a table has, and how its rows are laid out across them. The side pane lists the statements and the levers. Course twelve pulls them: compacting small files, and clustering rows so that a query can skip most of a table.

Before fraudsters spend a stolen card number, they test it.
