They try tiny amounts, a euro or two, at online shops the card has never used, many times in a few minutes, usually at night, to find out which numbers still work. It is called card testing, and it leaves a pattern a bank can see. Ring dot py, in the editor, looks for it in silver card transactions on one night, the twenty second of October: authorizations before five in the morning, grouped by card, keeping the cards with more than three. Six cards come back, and they look nothing like a customer. Each made eleven authorizations, within six to twelve minutes. Together they total only thirteen to sixteen euros. Some were declined, up to seven of eleven, and each card touched eight to eleven different merchants. The last line spells out one card, K003529: eleven authorizations between ten past two and nineteen minutes past, each between fifty six cents and two euros. The plot draws them, one bar per authorization. Nobody buys eleven things worth a euro each at eleven shops in nine minutes. Six cards at the same minutes of the same night is not chance either: it is one ring, testing a batch of numbers. That is what this course will catch, first with a rule, then with a model. And there is one thing we cannot know yet: whether these six were really fraud. That only comes later, as chargebacks.

The simplest detector is a rule, and banks start there because anyone can read it. Velocity dot sql states one: flag an authorization when its card has made more than five in the last ten minutes. The window function in the editor counts, for every authorization, the same card's authorizations in the ten minutes before it, a range over time, not a number of rows. A rule is only worth what it catches, so the query checks it against the only truth the bank has: September's chargebacks, the transactions cardholders later disputed as fraud. It runs on six nights, each ring's night and the night before it. On the twelfth of September the rule flags twenty eight authorizations, and all twenty eight were fraud. On the twenty sixth, thirty four, all fraud. On the nights before, nothing. So the rule never cried wolf. But each ring made sixty fraudulent authorizations, and the rule caught only about half: a card's first five authorizations in a burst can never be past five. On the twenty second of October it flags thirty six, and the fraud column says zero, not because they are innocent, but because October's chargebacks have not arrived yet. A label always comes late. The side pane shows the rule day by day, and the window it counts. A rule that runs once a day finds a ring the morning after. Next, the same rule, running as the authorizations arrive.

The rule in SQL answers the morning after. Card testing is over in a quarter of an hour, so the bank wants the flag while it is still happening. Stream dot py, in the editor, runs the same rule as a Structured Streaming query over bronze card authorizations, as they arrive. It groups them into ten minute windows that start every five minutes, per card, and keeps any window with more than five authorizations. Those flags are written to gold fraud flags. Two words carry the idea. A window is the ten minutes being counted. A watermark, thirty minutes here, is how late an authorization may still arrive and be counted: once a window is more than thirty minutes behind the newest authorization seen, it is closed, its flags are appended once, and they are never revised. Here the stream runs with an available now trigger: it processes everything that has arrived, then stops, so the course can read the result. Run every few minutes, or continuously, it is the same code. The terminal shows the flags, a night to a row. On the twelfth of September, eleven windows over six cards, between five past three and twenty past. On the twenty sixth, fourteen windows over five cards. On the twenty second of October, twelve windows over the six cards of section one, between five past two and twenty five past, the busiest window holding eleven authorizations. The side pane shows the windows and the watermark. A rule only knows one signal, though. Next, the features a model can weigh together.

A rule looks at one signal. A model can weigh several, but first they have to be computed, the same way, for every authorization: those are features. Features dot py, in the editor, builds them in one SQL statement over silver, into a table in the ml schema, ml card features. For each authorization: auths ten m, the card's authorizations in the ten minutes before it, the rule's own number. Online, whether the card was not present. Tiny amount, under two euros, the size of a test charge. Night, before five in the morning. And one more column, fraud, the label: whether a chargeback later named this authorization. Only September has labels; October's twenty second is there to be scored, not to learn from. The terminal counts it: eighteen thousand four hundred and eighty rows over six days. On the twelfth of September, six thousand three hundred and forty three authorizations, sixty of them fraud. On the twenty sixth, six thousand three hundred and forty six, sixty fraud. The average velocity is about one: almost every authorization is the only one its card made in ten minutes, which is exactly why the rings stand out. Because the table lives in Unity Catalog, it has an owner, grants and lineage like any other: the side pane lists what each feature means. Next, the model that learns from it.

A model is trained on the past to judge the future, and the past has to be kept apart from the test, or the score means nothing. Train dot py trains a logistic regression with scikit-learn, on the laptop, on the twelfth of September's features, and tests it on the twenty sixth, a night it has never seen. MLflow, which the workspace hosts, records the run: its parameters, its metrics and the trained model itself, in an experiment in the workspace. The model is also registered in Unity Catalog as globalbank dev ml card fraud, so it has an owner, grants and versions like a table. The terminal shows what matters. Trained on six thousand three hundred and forty three authorizations, sixty of them fraud; tested on six thousand three hundred and forty six, sixty fraud. Precision one, recall one: every authorization it flagged on the twenty sixth was fraud, and it flagged every fraudulent one. Before celebrating: these rings were planted by the course's own generator, small charges at night at new online shops, and that makes them easy to separate. Real fraud never scores perfectly. The weights say what the model learned: a tiny amount counts most, plus five point one four, then night, plus four point five three, then online, then the card's velocity. That is the same pattern section one saw by eye, now as numbers. The run is registered as version one. The side pane traces it: the run, its parameters, its metrics, the model. Next, how version one becomes the model the bank actually uses.

Training registered version one of globalbank dev ml card fraud in Unity Catalog. A version is not yet a decision: a bank may train many, and only one should be scoring real card payments. Unity Catalog marks that one with an alias, a name that points at a version. Registry dot py, in the editor, lists the model's versions and their aliases. The first command shows version one, ready, with no alias: nothing uses it yet. The second sets the alias champion on version one, and the listing now says so. From here on, everything that scores, the next section first, loads the model as card fraud at champion, never as version one. That is the whole point. When a better model is trained, it becomes version two, and it is tested beside the champion. Promoting it means moving the alias from one to two: one call, no change to any code that scores, and moving it back is just as quick if the new model misbehaves. Because the model lives in Unity Catalog, it is governed like the bank's tables: it has an owner, grants decide who may load it or move its alias, and its lineage shows the features it was trained on. The side pane shows the versions, and the alias that points at one of them. Next, the champion meets a night it has never seen: the twenty second of October.

The twenty second of October has no labels: its chargebacks have not arrived. This is what a fraud model is for, judging the authorizations nobody has judged yet. Score dot py, in the editor, reads that day's rows from ml card features, loads card fraud at champion from Unity Catalog, and gives each authorization a score between zero and one: the model's estimate that it is fraud. It keeps those at or above a threshold, nought point nine here, and appends them to ml fraud scores, for the analysts. One honest note about where this runs. On this workspace a Python function inside Spark does not start, so the scoring runs on the laptop, with the model loaded from the registry. On a full workspace the same model scores inside a stream or a job, as a Spark user defined function. The terminal shows the night. Five thousand five hundred and ninety three authorizations scored; sixty six flagged. They are the six cards of section one, eleven authorizations each, all of them, from ten past two, every score one. Compare the rule: it flagged thirty six of these sixty six, because a card's first five authorizations can never be over five. The model weighs the tiny amount, the hour and the online shop, so it flags the first authorization too, when only one card has been tested so far. The side pane traces the path: the features, the champion, the scores, and the flagged cards. Next: what the threshold costs.

Every flag lands in a queue that an analyst works through, and every analyst hour costs money. The threshold decides how long that queue is. Lower it, and the model flags more: more fraud caught, and more innocent customers to call. Raise it, and the queue is short, but some fraud slips past. Tradeoff dot py, in the editor, scores the twenty sixth of September, a night with labels, at five thresholds, and counts for each: the queue, the fraud caught, precision, recall, and the money in the fraud it caught. Six thousand three hundred and forty six authorizations; sixty fraud, worth seventy four euros seventy one. From nought point five to nought point nine seven, the answer does not change: a queue of sixty, all sixty caught, precision one, recall one. Only at nought point nine nine does the model start to miss: fifty five caught, recall nought point nine two. Real data never looks like this. The planted rings are cleanly separable, and on a real bank's authorizations the curve bends long before nought point nine nine. That bend is what the bank's fraud team chooses a point on, and this table is how to show it to them. One more number deserves a second look: the fraud here is worth seventy five euros. Card testing never costs much by itself. The money is in what comes after it, the stolen cards used for real, so catching the test early is what saves the money. The side pane draws the trade. Catching fraud is finished. Next course: running all of this every night, without anyone typing a command.

Everything Global Bank's lakehouse does, it has done because someone typed a command. A bank's numbers cannot depend on that. Every night, the day's files must become balances, statements and fraud flags, in the right order, whether anyone is awake or not. On Databricks that is a Lakeflow Job: a set of tasks, each one a pipeline, a SQL file on the warehouse or a Python script, with the order between them declared. Nightly dot yml, in the editor, declares globalbank nightly. Its first task is the pipeline from course seven, bronze and silver. After it, three tasks that only need silver: gold accounts, the daily balances, and the fraud rule. Statements wait for balances. Last, a check, a small Python script that waits for all of them. Job dot py, in the terminal, reads this file, fills in what only the workspace knows, the pipeline's id and the warehouse, uploads the SQL and the check, and creates the job. It prints each task and what it waits for: pipeline first; accounts, balances and flags after the pipeline; statements after balances; check after accounts, statements and flags. The side pane draws that graph. Three tasks can run at once, inside Free Edition's limit of five. The file is YAML in the shape a Declarative Automation Bundle expects, so course eleven can deploy this same file without a script. Next, run it.

Creating a job runs nothing. Job dot py run, in the editor, asks the Jobs API to run it now, waits until the run has a result, and then reads the run back: its trigger, and every task's final state. The terminal shows the first run of globalbank nightly. Result: success. Trigger: one time, meaning someone asked for it. Six tasks. The pipeline ran first, then accounts, balances and flags, then statements, then the check, every one of them a success. Nothing here was typed in order by a person: the job read the dependencies and started each task the moment the tasks before it had finished. Each task ran on serverless compute: the pipeline on its own, the SQL tasks on the warehouse, and the check as a serverless Python task. The side pane draws the run on the same graph as the job, each task coloured by its result. A run like this is what the bank's morning starts from: if it succeeded, the balances, statements and fraud flags are the night's. But a run started by hand still needs a hand. The data arrives on its own schedule, so the next section lets the data start the job.

The card scheme's clearing file arrives when it arrives: usually overnight, sometimes late. Starting the job at a fixed hour either waits too long or runs before the file is there. A file arrival trigger starts the job when a new file lands. In the editor, nightly dot yml gains a trigger: file arrival, on the settlements landing volume. The terminal deploys the change; the job is updated. The trigger checks the folder about once a minute, and it needs a moment to start watching, so the next command waits ninety seconds. Then the first of November's clearing file lands: one file. Nobody runs the job. Job dot py wait watches for a run the trigger starts, and reads it when it finishes: result success, trigger file arrival, six tasks, every one a success. The pipeline picked up the new file, and everything after it was rebuilt from it. The side pane follows it: the file lands, the trigger sees it, and a run starts, with its tasks' states beside it. The job now follows the data, not the clock. But what if the data never comes, or comes late? A job that waits for a file can also run without it, and the next section is what happens then.

Some nights the clearing file does not come. The job must not quietly publish yesterday's balances as today's, so the check in the editor refuses: if no settlement has cleared on the night it is processing, it stops the run with an error. Here the night is the thirty first of October, and its clearing file has not landed. The terminal runs the job. The pipeline, accounts, balances, flags and statements all succeed, on the data they have. The check fails, twice, because the job retried it once: no clearing file for the thirty first, the gold tables are stale. The run is marked failed, and its owner would be emailed. Then the file arrives: the thirty first's clearing file lands. Now the question is how to finish the night. Starting a new run would work, but a repair is better: it re-runs tasks inside the same failed run, so the night keeps one run, one history, one record of what went wrong and how it was fixed. Which tasks? Not just the check. The missing file only reaches the balances through the pipeline, so the repair re-runs from the pipeline down, every task that depends on it. Job dot py repair does that, and the same run ends in success: every task now shows two attempts, and the check three. The side pane lines the run up before and after the repair. A repair re-runs tasks, and some tasks were not written to run twice. That is the next section.

A job runs more than once. A trigger fires twice, someone re-runs a failed night, a repair re-runs half of one. Every task must therefore give the same result however many times it runs: that is called idempotent. This section adds a task that is not. Month end dot sql, in the editor, writes the figures the ledger closes the month on: for each month, how many statements, and the total of their closing balances. It inserts them into gold month end. The job gains it as its last task, and the terminal runs the job twice, as a retry would. Both runs succeed, seven tasks each. Then the table, as the ledger reads it: October, six thousand four hundred and forty two statements, thirty four million nine hundred and fifty one thousand euros. And October again, the same numbers. Two rows for one month, so anything that sums this table now reports October's money twice. Nothing failed, and no test of a single run would catch it: each run did exactly what it was told. The fault is the statement, insert into, which adds rows every time it runs. The side pane shows the two rows, and why a re-run doubled the month. Next, the fix, and a way to tell the task which month it is closing.

Two changes make month end safe to re-run. First, the job takes a parameter, run date, the night it is processing, and passes it to the check. The check, in Python, counts what cleared that day, and hands a value on to later tasks: the month, here twenty twenty six dash ten. These are task values, small results one task sets and another reads. Second, month end dot sql, in the editor, now inserts with replace where month equals that month. Instead of adding rows, it replaces whatever the table held for the month with the new figures, in one atomic write. The terminal runs the job twice, with run date the thirty first of October; both succeed. Job dot py output check prints what the check said in the last run: on the thirty first of October, five thousand three hundred and fifty eight settlements cleared, and there are six thousand four hundred and forty two statements. Then gold month end: one row for October. Not one row added: one row in total. The replace also removed the duplicate the last section left behind, because it replaces everything for the month. However many times the job runs for October, October has one row. The side pane follows the values: the parameter into the check, the month out of it, into month end. Last in this course: whose name the job runs under, and who hears when it fails.

Every run reads and writes the bank's tables as someone, and Unity Catalog checks that someone's grants. Nightly dot yml, in the editor, now says who: run as, and, on failure, whom to email. The terminal deploys it, and job dot py who reads the job back from the workspace: run as ana at globalbank dot example, and on failure, email the same address. In this course Ana is the only user, so the job runs as her and tells her when it breaks. The second table in the side pane is what a real bank does instead, from the documentation: a job runs as a service principal, an identity for software, not for a person. It is granted exactly what the job needs, and it does not vanish when its author changes teams or leaves the bank. Free Edition has no account console in which to make one, so this course stops at the person. The nightly job is complete: triggered by the clearing file, ordered by its dependencies, safe to re-run, parameterised, and owned. But it exists in the workspace because a script put it there, and anyone can still change it there with a click. Course eleven makes the repository the only way it changes.

The nightly job from course ten exists in two places. Resources nightly dot yml, in the repository, is the version that was reviewed. The job in the workspace is the version that actually runs. Job dot py copied the first into the second once, and nothing keeps them equal after that. Drift dot py, in the editor, shows how they come apart. It plays a colleague who opens the job in the workspace's web page and changes two settings: up to three runs at once, and a tag saying it was edited by hand. The script makes the same API call the page makes. Then it compares the job as deployed from the repository with the job as the workspace now holds it. Two settings differ: max concurrent runs, one in the repository, three in the workspace; and tags, none in the repository, edited by hand in the workspace. The last line is the real problem: resources nightly dot yml is unchanged, so nothing in the repository records the edit. No review saw it, no history explains it, and the next deploy from the repository will silently undo it, or someone will copy the edited job by hand and the two will drift further. The side pane puts the two copies side by side. The cure is to make the repository the only way anything in the workspace changes, and to deploy all of it, pipeline, job and dashboard, as one unit. That unit is a bundle.

A Declarative Automation Bundle, formerly called Databricks Asset Bundles, is a folder in the repository that describes everything a project deploys, and the Databricks CLI deploys it. Databricks dot yml, in the editor, is its root. It names the bundle, globalbank. It includes every file under resources, one per workspace object: the pipeline from course seven, and the nightly job from course ten, the same file, now read by the CLI instead of by a script. It declares a variable, the warehouse's id, looked up by the warehouse's name when the bundle deploys, so no id is ever written into the repository. And it declares a target, dev, the default. A dot gitignore keeps the virtual environments and the landing data out: the bundle uploads what git would track, and nothing else. The terminal runs databricks bundle validate. The CLI reads every file, resolves the includes, checks the result against the bundle schema, and reports where it would deploy: target dev, as Ana, into a folder of her own under dot bundle, globalbank, dev. Validation OK. Nothing has been deployed: validate only reads. The side pane traces the parts: the root file includes the resources, the resources point at the code, and the code is synced into the bundle's folder in the workspace. Next, what the bundle will create there.

Each file under resources describes one workspace object in YAML, using the same fields as the API that creates it. Dashboard dot yml, in the editor, adds the third: the statements dashboard from course eight. Its definition stays where it already lives, in dashboards slash statements dot lvdash dot json, and the warehouse it queries is the variable from the root file. Databricks bundle summary, in the terminal, lists what the bundle would manage, without deploying anything. Three resources. A dashboard, globalbank statements. A job, globalbank nightly. A pipeline, globalbank pipeline. Each is shown with the name it will get in this target. In dev, every name is prefixed with dev and the user's short name: dev underscore ana underscore globalbank nightly. The prefix is the point of a development target: two engineers can deploy the same bundle into one workspace without their jobs and pipelines colliding, and anyone looking at the workspace can tell a developer's copy from the real one. Each one says not deployed: the summary only reads. The side pane maps each key in the YAML to the workspace object it becomes. One folder now describes the pipeline, the nightly job and the dashboard. Next, the same folder deployed two ways: for development, and for production.

One bundle, more than one place to deploy it: those places are targets. Databricks dot yml, in the editor, now has two. Dev is in development mode: names prefixed with the user, schedules and triggers paused so a developer's copy never runs by itself at night, and the pipeline writing to globalbank dev. Prod is in production mode: no prefix, triggers live, the catalog variable set to globalbank prod, and a root path fixed in one place, so there is only ever one deployed copy. The terminal validates both and prints the first five lines of each: the same bundle, target dev, deploying into dot bundle slash globalbank slash dev; and target prod, deploying into dot bundle slash globalbank slash prod. Both validate. The table on the right lists what each target changes, and the note says what this course does not do. Free Edition has one workspace and allows one pipeline of each type, so prod is validated here but not deployed. In a real bank, prod is another workspace, with its own host written into the prod target, and nobody deploys to it from a laptop. Next, deploying dev for real, and running the nightly job the bundle created.

The workspace was reset before this section, so nothing the bank runs exists there yet: no pipeline, no job, no dashboard. Databricks bundle deploy, in the terminal, creates all of it from the repository in one command. First it uploads the bundle's files, the pipelines, the SQL, the check script, into the bundle's own folder in the workspace: ninety six files. Then it creates each resource, filling in what only the workspace knows, the pipeline's id inside the job's first task, the warehouse found by name. The dashboard, the pipeline and the nightly job: three created, nothing changed or deleted. The CLI also keeps a record of what it deployed, so the next deploy changes only what differs, and deletes what was removed from the YAML. Resources nightly dot yml, in the editor, is the same file course ten wrote; its first task points at the pipeline by reference, resources dot pipelines dot globalbank pipeline dot id, which the deploy resolves. Then databricks bundle run globalbank nightly starts the job and follows it to the end: dev ana globalbank nightly, terminated, success. The whole nightly run, built from nothing by two commands, from code that is in the repository and nowhere else. Change the YAML, deploy again, and the workspace follows. Edit the job by hand, and the next deploy puts it back. The side pane follows the deploy, step by step, into the run. Code that deploys itself needs to be trusted, so next: tests.

A transform that is only ever run inside a pipeline can only be tested by running the pipeline. So the transforms the bank depends on most move into plain functions of DataFrames, in globalbank slash transforms dot py: velocity, the card's authorizations in the last ten minutes, which the fraud rule counts, and latest change, the newest record per key by the source's sequence, which the core system's changes need. The functions take a DataFrame and return one; they do not know where it came from. That makes them testable anywhere Spark runs. Test transforms dot py, in the editor, builds tiny DataFrames by hand, six authorizations a minute apart and a seventh half an hour later, and checks the counts the window must give: one, two, three, four, five, six, then one again. The second test hands two changes to one customer in the wrong order and checks that the higher sequence wins. These run on a local PySpark, in a virtual environment of their own, on the laptop, with no workspace at all: two passed, in about fifteen seconds. One more test runs the same velocity function through Databricks Connect, on the workspace's real silver card transactions for the twenty second of October, and checks it finds the six cards of the ring: one passed. Many small, fast tests at the bottom, run on every change; a few real ones at the top. The side pane draws that pyramid. Last: making those tests and the deploy run by themselves.

Everything so far was run from a laptop. In a bank, nobody deploys to production from a laptop: a change goes through a pull request, a reviewer approves it, and an automated pipeline tests it and deploys it. Deploy dot yml, in the editor, is a GitHub Actions workflow that does that. On every pull request it installs PySpark and runs the unit tests, the fast part of the pyramid. When a change is merged to main, and only if the tests passed, a second job installs the Databricks CLI and runs databricks bundle deploy, target prod. It deploys as a service principal, an identity for software, whose OAuth credentials are stored as GitHub secrets, never in the repository. This part is documented, not run: creating a service principal's secret needs the account console, which Free Edition does not have. What can run here, does: the terminal validates the prod target, exactly as the workflow's deploy step would see it, and validation is OK. The side pane follows a change from pull request to tests to merge to deploy, with the documented step marked. The bank's lakehouse is now code: reviewed, tested, deployed the same way every time, and never edited by hand. One course remains: running it for real, what it costs, and keeping it fast as it grows.

A lakehouse that runs every night costs money every night, and the bank will ask how much. Databricks measures compute in DBUs, Databricks units, and records every one in a system table, system billing usage: what was used, by which product, when. Cost dot py, in the editor, sums it by product since the twenty seventh of October, when this course's lakehouse moved to this workspace. Eleven DBUs in all. Six point seven for interactive serverless compute: every Databricks Connect script in the course. Four point one six for default storage, the managed tables' files. A little for predictive optimization, the platform's own table maintenance, and for Genie. Two things to read carefully. First, the bill is late. It reaches midnight, and there is no row yet for the pipelines, the warehouse or the jobs that ran since: usage arrives in this table hours after the work. Cost reporting therefore looks at yesterday, never at the last hour. Second, this course quotes DBUs, not money. What a DBU costs depends on the cloud, the product and the contract, so the price is the bank's to apply. The side pane plots the DBUs by product and says what each line of the bill is. The cheapest DBU is the one never spent, and a lot of compute is spent reading files that did not need reading. Next: small files.

Every time Auto Loader ingests a batch, it writes new files into the bronze table. It never adds rows to an existing file: Delta files are written once and never changed. So a table fed often grows by many small files, and every query that reads it has to open each one, paying a request and a footer read per file, however little data is inside. This section lands seven days of card authorizations, one ingest per day, the way course three did. Files dot py counts what the table is made of: bronze card auths is eight files, eight tenths of a megabyte, about a hundred kilobytes each. Small, and this is only a week. A bank landing a file every fifteen minutes writes ninety six batches a day, every day. Optimize dot py, in the editor, runs one command: optimize. It rewrites the small files into fewer, larger ones, and commits the change as one new version of the table: eight files removed, one added. Counted again, bronze card auths is one file of seven tenths of a megabyte, smaller in total, because one file compresses better than eight. No row changed, and a query reading the table now opens one file instead of eight. The side pane plots the file count before and after. Compaction is the price of fresh data, paid later and in bulk. But how the rows are laid out inside the files matters too, which is the next section.

Fewer files help every query. Which rows sit in which file helps the queries that filter. Every Delta file records the minimum and maximum of its columns, and a query that filters skips any file whose range cannot match. Whether it can skip depends on how the rows were laid out. Cluster dot py, in the editor, copies bronze card auths into two silver tables, with a small target file size so a week of data spans several files. The first is laid out as the rows arrived. The second declares cluster by merchant ID and authorization time: liquid clustering, which keeps rows with nearby keys in the same files as the table is optimized, and can change its keys later without rewriting by hand. Then it runs the question the supermarket chain M0001 asks: its authorizations on the third of October, on each table, and reads from the query history how many files each read and skipped, waiting until the history has both. By arrival: one file read, none skipped; that file holds everything, so nothing could be skipped. Clustered: one file read, five skipped, because only one file's range of merchants and times could contain the answer. M0001 is a fifth of all authorizations, the skew the generator planted, which is exactly when a layout pays. On a bank's years of data, five skipped files become thousands. The side pane plots read against skipped. Optimize and clustering are work someone has to schedule. Next: the platform scheduling it itself.

The last two sections ran optimize by hand. Predictive optimization is the platform doing that work itself, for managed tables in Unity Catalog: it watches how each table is used and runs optimize, vacuum and statistics when it judges they pay for themselves, billed as its own product, a line section one's bill already showed. Predictive dot py, in the editor, asks three questions. Is it on? The silver schema says enable, inherited from the metastore, so every managed table here is covered without any setting of ours. What has it run on globalbank dev? It records its operations in a system table, system storage predictive optimization operations history, and for this catalog there are none yet: these tables are hours old, and it acts on tables that have lived long enough to show a pattern. And what happened to the clustered table from the last section? Its own history shows two creates and four optimize operations: this step was replayed twice, and each time cluster dot py ran one optimize and Delta ran one more by itself. The table on the right lists who does what: compaction, clustering, vacuum and statistics, by hand in this course, and by predictive optimization once it is on and the tables are old enough. Honest operations means knowing which is which. That is all of the bank: one last look at it, finished.

Here is Global Bank's lakehouse, finished: the map from course one, every part now lit. On the left, the sources: the card scheme's authorization and clearing files, the core banking system's changes and postings, the mobile app's events. They land as files in Unity Catalog volumes. Bronze keeps every record exactly as it came, complete. Silver makes it correct: one row per real thing, duplicates and late arrivals handled, the core system's history kept, customers' personal data masked. Gold makes it ready, shaped for one use each: daily balances, statements, card spend, the regulator's report, fraud flags. On the right, the consumers: the dashboard, the overdraft alert, the analysts' fraud queue. Underneath it all, one declared pipeline, a nightly job that the clearing file starts, a bundle that deploys all of it from the repository, and tests that run before anything ships. And everything on this map ran, on a free workspace. The side pane shows two of its real results. And the champion model's night of the twenty second of October, from course nine: five thousand five hundred and ninety three authorizations scored, sixty six flagged. One section is left: where to go from here.

This course built one bank, deeply, on a free workspace, and so it left things out. The table on screen is where each part of the bank goes next, with what the Free Edition limitations page said on the twenty eighth of October. Gold, for people who do not write SQL: Genie answers questions in plain language over the gold tables; it already appears on this workspace's bill. A branch's customer screen: Databricks Apps can serve one, reading gold; Free Edition allows three, each running for a day per start. A balance that must be exact this second, not tonight: Lakebase puts a Postgres database beside the lakehouse; Free Edition allows one project. The fraud model, called on every single payment: Model Serving puts the champion behind an endpoint; Free Edition allows it, without GPUs. Silver's quality, watched over time: data profiling, formerly called Lakehouse Monitoring. Statements shared with a partner bank: Delta Sharing. The limitations page does not mention those two. For everything else the platform does, the companion course, databricks data engineer ct, covers it broadly, without a workspace. This one showed what all of it looks like when it really runs, with real numbers, in a bank that adds up. Thank you for building it.
